extracted.intended_audience: corporate IP managers, patent counsel, policymakers, and business strategists interested in patent risk mitigation
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the practice, rationale, business models, and strategies of defensive patent aggregation—buying patents to prevent their use in assertions against operating companies. Covers motivations (litigation cost, NPE activity), third‑party aggregator models, and specific defensive strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defensive patent aggregation (DPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: DPA is the practice of purchasing patents or patent rights to keep such patents out of the hands of entities that would assert them against operating companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is risk mitigation—preventing assertion against operating companies by removing patents from potential litigants or ensuring they are subject to defensive licensing arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offensive patent aggregation (OPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: OPA is the purchasing of patents in order to assert them against companies that would use the inventions protected by such patents (operating companies) and to grant licenses to these operating companies in return for licensing fees or royalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with DPA: OPA acquires to monetize and assert; OPA can be practiced by operating companies or non‑practicing entities (NPEs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Operating companies' motivations for acquiring patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Operating companies must often defend themselves against claims of patent infringement. To prevent such litigations, operating companies sometimes purchase patents in technologies which they use or develop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other motivations include the ability to counter‑assert if sued and pooling efforts/financial resources with peers to purchase patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third‑party defensive aggregator business model
rubrics_metrics.description: A third‑party—the aggregator—purchases the patents or patent rights strictly to mitigate the risk and cost of litigation associated with NPEs and provides licenses to members against a fixed annual membership fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This business model emerged around 2008 and separates aggregation activity from operating companies, offering collective protection to members for a subscription fee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defensive aggregation as aggregation of defensive strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Defensive patent aggregation has evolved to be more accurately described as the aggregation of defensive strategies from patent assertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implies DPA may combine multiple tactics (licensing, challenges, cross‑licensing) rather than only buying patents to hold them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pro‑active cross‑licensing
rubrics_metrics.description: Pro‑active cross‑licensing between patent holders so that any patents transferred to an NPE will be licensed already.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example implementation: LOT Network—prevents patents from becoming weapons when transferred to NPEs by ensuring licenses travel with transfers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group buying and licensing
rubrics_metrics.description: Group buying and licensing to obtain licenses for groups of companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include AST (Allied Security Trust) and RPX, which pool purchasing power to acquire patent rights or licenses on behalf of members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre‑emptive patent challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre‑emptive patent challenges of patents held by NPEs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example organization: Unified Patents, which challenges problematic patents before they can be asserted or monetized against operating companies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale — high litigation costs and unpredictability
rubrics_metrics.description: The cost of defending against a patent infringement suit (as of 2004 in the U.S.) is typically $1 million or more before trial, and $4 million or more for a complete defense; combined with settlement/licensing costs, total costs are often much higher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High costs and the unpredictability of jury trials encourage defendants to settle even non‑meritorious suits, creating economic pressure to pursue defensive aggregation to reduce exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and behavior of non‑practicing entities (NPEs)
rubrics_metrics.description: NPEs (also called patent trolls) acquire patents for the sole purpose of licensing and asserting their patent rights; NPE litigation share grew from 2.6% of filed cases in 2000 to 16.6% in 2007.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike operating/product companies, NPEs are not susceptible to counter‑assertion, making them potent adversaries; NPEs include single‑inventor assertion firms, licensing and enforcement companies, litigation financiers, and patent aggregators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defensive responses to NPE activity
rubrics_metrics.description: NPE defense methods include defensive patent aggregation, cooperative purchasing efforts (defensive patent pools and buying consortia), outright purchasing of patents, settlement, and litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of entities engaged in these defenses include RPX Corporation and various buying consortia; the suite of defenses can be used in combination depending on strategy and resources.
